       DEFENDANT META PLATFORMS, INC.’S RESPONSE IN OPPOSITION TO
           PLAINTIFF’S MOTION FOR LEAVE TO SERVE FOUR LIMITED
      INTERROGATORIES ON META PLATFORMS, INC. BEFORE THE RULE 26(f)
                               CONFERENCE

     Defendant Meta Platforms, Inc., (“Meta”) by and through its undersigned counsel, hereby

  respectfully opposes Plaintiff Marvelle J. Ballentine’s Motion for Leave to Serve Four Limited

  Interrogatories on Meta Before the Rule 26(f) Conference. Dkt. No. 54. In support of its response,

  Meta states the following:

     I.      Procedural History

          In this action, Plaintiff seeks to hold Defendants National Center for Missing & Exploited

  Children (“NCMEC”) and Katie Hall (collectively, the “NCMEC Defendants”) liable for

  responding to draft subpoenas that Plaintiff sent to NCMEC, which each requested “a document

  sufficient to show whether NCMEC received or maintains any CyberTipline report concerning (1)

  Marvelle    J.    Ballentine;   (2)    Jay   Ballentine,   and/or   the   account-level   identifier

  jaychizza@icloud.com.” FAC ¶ 56. He also seeks to hold Meta liable for purportedly conspiring

  with the NCMEC Defendants to send the responses to the draft subpoenas.


                                                    1

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD               Document 73        Filed 09/17/26      Page 2 of 7 PageID# 746




              Plaintiff first raised his claims against the NCMEC Defendants in a separate action in this

  district. See Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, et al., No. 1:26-cv-1341,

  Dkt. No. 1 (E.D. Va. May 19, 2026). After moving to dismiss Plaintiff’s Complaint there, the

  NCMEC Defendants filed a Motion to Stay Discovery. Id., Dkt. No. 11 at 3-4. The court granted

  their motion, staying all discovery pending resolution of the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to

  Dismiss. Id., Dkt. No. 15. Plaintiff then voluntarily dismissed that action and reasserted his claim

  against the NCMEC Defendants in the instant action, adding Meta as a Defendant. Id., Dkt. No.

  21.

              After the NCMEC Defendants renewed their Motion to Dismiss, Plaintiff filed a motion

  seeking leave to serve three interrogatories on NCMEC prior to any Rule 26(f) conference. See

  Dkt. No. 15. The three proposed interrogatories asked whether NCMEC received a CyberTipline

  report associated with each of the three identifiers listed in the proposed subpoenas Plaintiff sent

  to NCMEC. Id. NCMEC opposed Plaintiff’s request. See Dkt. No. 33.

              Similarly, after Meta filed its Motion to Dismiss (Dkt. No. 21), Plaintiff filed the instant

  motion, seeking leave to serve four interrogatories on Meta prior to any Rule 26(f) conference,

  closely mirroring his prior requests directed to NCMEC. Dkt. No. 54. Plaintiff’s proposed

  interrogatories to Meta ask whether Meta submitted any CyberTipline regarding his Facebook

  account and, whether any such report submitted by Meta identified any of the three identifiers

  provided by Plaintiff. Id.

        II.      Legal Standard

              Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(d)(1) provides that a “party may not seek discovery from any source

  before the parties have conferred as required by Rule 26(f), except. . . when authorized. . . by court

  order.” “A district court has wide latitude in controlling discovery.” Rowland v. Am. Gen. Fin.,

  Inc., 340 F.3d 187, 195 (4th Cir. 2003). “In rare circumstances, the court may authorize expedited


                                                       2

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 73       Filed 09/17/26      Page 3 of 7 PageID# 747




  discovery upon a showing of good cause.” Thornock v. JES Found. Repair & Groundworks, No.

  7:23-CV-00638, 2023 WL 12012073, at *1 (W.D. Va. Oct. 25, 2023) (internal quotation marks

  omitted).

            Although “the Federal Rules of Civil Procedure do not specify a standard for assessing

  when to grant Motions for Expedited Discovery, and the Fourth Circuit has not established one,”

  courts in this district have applied “a modified preliminary injunction test to assess whether

  expedited discovery is warranted.” Arthur J. Gallagher & Co. v. Markfeld, No. 3:25-cv-885, 2026

  WL 2186600, at *9 (E.D. Va. July 29, 2026) (internal quotation marks omitted). Under this test the

  court considers “whether the Plaintiff has made a strong showing of merits,” and whether

  irreparable harm exists absent expedited discovery. Id. (internal quotation marks omitted). Such

  “relief outside of the federal rules should be limited to unusual circumstances.” Id.

     III.      Argument

            Plaintiff’s Motion does not establish that this case presents an “unusual circumstance”

  warranting expedited discovery outside the federal rules. Indeed, the opposite is true: Plaintiff has

  not shown a strong likelihood of success on the merits or any irreparable harm if his request for

  early discovery is denied.

            A. Plaintiff Is Not Likely To Succeed on the Merits

            Meta’s Motion to Dismiss demonstrates that Plaintiff cannot show a strong likelihood of

  success on the merits as to his claims against Meta. See Dkt. Nos. 21, 22, 30, 39. As Meta explained

  in its Motion to Dismiss, the FAC’s allegations fail to state any claim for relief against Meta

  because, among other things, Plaintiff fails to plausibly allege the existence of a conspiracy

  between Meta and the NCMEC Defendants. Even if the discovery Plaintiff requests could be

  considered in resolving Meta’s Motion to Dismiss (it cannot), the information sought cannot rescue

  the FAC’s deficient allegations.


                                                   3

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 73        Filed 09/17/26      Page 4 of 7 PageID# 748




         Courts have recognized that discovery prior to resolution of case-dispositive motions to

  dismiss are inappropriate, as is the case here. See, e.g., Rivers v. United States, No. 6:18-cv-00061,

  2020 WL 1469475, at *1 (W.D. Va. Jan. 24, 2020) (finding that “early discovery is not reasonable

  at this stage of the proceeding” and “good cause” exists “to stay all discovery” until after the court

  “determines which of Plaintiff’s claims, if any, survive” the pending motions to dismiss); cf.

  Colonial River Wealth Advisors, LLC v. Cambridge Inv. Rsch., Inc., No. 3:22-cv-717, 2023 WL

  4936708, at *1 (E.D. Va. June 5, 2023) (staying discovery pending resolution of motion to dismiss

  where the motion “would dispose of all the claims against [defendant]” and the “moving

  Defendants have made a colorable showing raising doubts as to the viability of Plaintiff’s

  complaint”). And, because Meta’s Motion to Dismiss tests only the sufficiency of the allegations

  in the FAC, any discovery would have no bearing on the resolution of Meta’s Motion to Dismiss.

  Meade v. Hicks, No. 3:21-cv-222, 2022 WL 433004, at *4 (E.D. Va. Feb. 11, 2022) (noting that

  “at the motion to dismiss stage, the Court generally only considers the well-pleaded factual

  allegations in the complaint”).

         B. Plaintiff Cannot Establish Irreparable Harm

         Plaintiff also cannot establish any irreparable harm from not receiving the discovery he

  requests now. In the event that either of Plaintiff’s claims against Meta survive Meta’s Motion to

  Dismiss, Plaintiff would be free to then seek discovery, after the parties have conferred pursuant

  to Rule 26(f).

     Notably, a different court in this district previously stayed all discovery pending resolution of

  the NCMEC Defendants’ Motion to Dismiss the first lawsuit that Plaintiff filed against them based

  on the same responses to Plaintiff’s draft subpoenas that are at issue in the present action.

  Ballentine v. Nat’l Ctr. for Missing & Exploited Children, et al., No. 1:26-cv-1341-MSN/WBP,




                                                    4

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD            Document 73         Filed 09/17/26      Page 5 of 7 PageID# 749




  Dkt. No. 15. Allowing Plaintiff to obtain early discovery in this new action (against either Meta or

  the NCMEC Defendants) would improperly reward Plaintiff’s procedural gamesmanship in

  voluntarily dismissing his first action only to re-file a substantially similar action to avoid both the

  stay of discovery and Rule 15’s requirement that he obtain leave before amending his complaint.

         C. Plaintiff’s Proffered Justification for Seeking Early Discovery Lacks Merit.

         Plaintiff appears to argue that any decision on Meta’s Motion to Dismiss without the

  requested discovery would be prejudicial to Plaintiff because Meta’s Motion to Dismiss

  purportedly raised a new factual issue; namely, whether NCMEC’s responses to Plaintiff’s draft

  subpoenas provided the “exact discovery” that Meta objected to in parallel cases that Plaintiff

  brought against Meta. Dkt. No. 55 at 4-5. But he is wrong. Meta’s Motion to Dismiss did not raise

  a new factual issue, it responded to Plaintiff’s allegations. Specifically, the FAC itself alleges that

  the “April 21, 2026 motions [i.e., Meta’s motions to stay discovery in the separate actions] were

  directed at the same discovery the April 9, 2026 materials [i.e., the proposed subpoenas to

  NCMEC] described.” FAC ¶ 127. The FAC further alleges that NCMEC’s letters “supplied. . . the

  precise subject scheduled for sworn examination” in Plaintiff’s upcoming deposition, which the

  motions to stay sought to prevent. FAC ¶ 133. To the extent Plaintiff disagrees with Meta’s

  characterizations of his FAC, he was free to raise that—and did in fact do so—in his Opposition

  to Meta’s Motion to Dismiss. See Dkt. No. 30 at 6 (arguing that the FAC did not admit that the

  letters from “NCMEC supplied exactly what Plaintiff requested”). That issue can be resolved based

  on the parties’ briefing on Meta’s Motion to Dismiss. Any further factual development would be

  wholly irrelevant for the purpose of evaluating the Motion to Dismiss, since the Court cannot

  consider evidence outside the pleadings. See Meade, 2022 WL 433004, at *4.




                                                     5

Case 1:26-cv-02331-RDA-IDD         Document 73       Filed 09/17/26      Page 6 of 7 PageID# 750




           Because the requested discovery does not impact the resolution of Meta’s Motion to

  Dismiss, the pendency of that motion cannot give rise to irreparable harm warranting premature

  discovery.

     IV.       Conclusion

     For the foregoing reasons, Meta respectfully requests that the Court deny Plaintiff’s Motion

  for Leave to Serve Four Limited Interrogatories on Meta Before the Rule 26(f) Conference.

  Dated: September 17, 2026
